questions.q: In a class of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>140</mn></math> students numbered <math><mn>1</mn></math> to<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>140</mn></math> , all even numbered students opted Mathematics course, those whose number is divisible by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>3</mn></math> opted Physics course and those whose number is divisible by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>5</mn></math> opted Chemistry course. Then the number of students who did not opt for any of the three courses is:
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
From the given 140 students, all even numbered students opted Mathematics M, hence, the number of students opted Mathematics is M≡1402=70, where x denotes the greatest integer function of x.

Similarly, the students who opted Physics are P≡1403=46

And, the students who opted Chemistry are C≡1405=28

Similarly, the students who opted Mathematics and Physics are the numbers which are divisible by both 2 & 3 i.e. 6, and their number is 1406=23

The students who opted Mathematics and Chemistry are the numbers which are divisible by both 2 & 5 i.e. 10, and their number is 14010=14

The students who opted Physics and Chemistry are the numbers which are divisible by both 3 & 5 i.e. 15, and their number is 14015=9

And, the students who opted all the three subjects are the numbers which are divisible by 2, 3 & 5 i.e. 30, and their number is 14030=4

Now, using
nP∪C∪M=nP+nC+nM-nP∩C-nC∩M-nM∩P+nP∩M∩C

=46+28+70-9-14-23+4

=102

Thus, 102 students have opted for atleast one of the three subjects.

Hence, number of students who did not opt for any of the three courses =140-102=38.

questions.q: Let $\mathrm{A}=\left\{x \in(0, \pi)-\left\{\frac{\pi}{2}\right\}: \log _{(2 / \pi)}|\sin x|+\log _{(2 / \pi)}|\cos x|=2\right\}$ and $\mathrm{B}=\{x \geqslant 0: \sqrt{x}(\sqrt{x}-4)-3|\sqrt{x}-2|+6=0\}$. Then $\mathrm{n}(\mathrm{A} \cup \mathrm{B})$ is equal to :
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{A}: \log _{2 \pi}|\sin \mathrm{x}|+\log _{2 \pi}|\cos \mathrm{x}|=2 \\ & \Rightarrow \log _{2 \pi}(|\sin \mathrm{x} \cdot \cos \mathrm{x}|)=2 \\ & \Rightarrow|\sin 2 \mathrm{x}|=\frac{8}{\pi^2}\end{aligned}$
Number of solution 4 $\text { B : let } \sqrt{\mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{t} \lt 2$ Then $\sqrt{x}(\sqrt{x}-4)+3(\sqrt{x}-2)+6=0\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \mathrm{t}^2-4 \mathrm{t}+3 \mathrm{t}-6+6=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{t}^2-\mathrm{t}=0, \mathrm{t}=0, \mathrm{t}=1 \\ & \mathrm{x}=0, \mathrm{x}=1 \end{aligned}$ again let $\sqrt{\mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{t} \gt 2$ then $\mathrm{t}^2-4 \mathrm{t}-3 \mathrm{t}+6+6=0\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \mathrm{t}^2-7 \mathrm{t}+12=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{t}=3,4 \\ & \mathrm{x}=9,16 \end{aligned}$ Total number of solutions $\mathrm{n}(\mathrm{~A} \cup \mathrm{~B})=4+4=8$

questions.q: If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>R</mi></math> is the smallest equivalence relation on the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>}</mo></math> such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>{</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>}</mo><mo>⊂</mo><mi>R</mi></math>, then the number of elements in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>R</mi></math> is ______.
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given: R=1,3,1,2

To make R as Reflexive, the required elements are 1,1, 2,2, 3,3 and 4,4

To make R as Symmetric, the required elements are 3,1 and 2,1

To make R as Transitive, the required elements are 3,2 and 2,3

So, 8 elements are required to make R an equivalence relation.

Hence, the total number of elements in R is 10.

Then the number of elements in the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>R</mi></math> is
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

A=1,3,4,6,9 & B=2,4,5,8,10

And relation is given by,

R=a1,b1,a2,b2:a1≤b2 and b1≤a2

Now taking cases for a1≤b2 we get,

a1=1, b2∈2,4,5,8,10→5 cases

a1=3, b2∈4,5,8,10→4 cases

a1=4, b2∈4,5,8,10→4 cases

a1=6, b2∈8,10→2 cases

a1=9, b2∈10→1 cases

So, total 16 cases will be there 

Now finding cases of b1≤a2 we get,

b1=2, a2∈3,4,6,9→4 cases

b1=4, a2∈4,6,9→3 cases

b1=5, a2∈6,9→2 cases

b1=8, a2∈9→1 cases

So, here total 10 cases,

Hence, total elements in relation =16×10=160

questions.q: Consider the relations R1 and R2 defined as aR1b⇔a2+b2=1 for all a,b,∈R and a,bR2c,d⇔a+d=b+c for all a,b,c,d∈N×N. Then
options: Neither <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> nor <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> is an equivalence relation
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

aR1b⇔a2+b2=1;a,b∈R

R1 is not reflexive as a,a∉aR1b

So, it is not equivalence.

Now, solving

a,bR2c,d⇔a+d=b+c;a,b,c,d∈N

Reflexive: a+b=b+a→True

Symmetric: a,bR2c,d

⇒a+d=b+c

⇒d+a=c+b

⇒c+b=d+a

⇒c,dR2a,b

Transitive: a,bR2c,d⇒a+d=b+c   ...i

c,dR2e,f⇒c+f=d+e   ...ii

Now, adding above equation we get,

⇒a+f=b+e

⇒a,bR2e,f

So, R2 is reflexive, symmetric and transitive

Hence only R2 is equivalence relation.

questions.solution:

If  <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi><mo>%</mo></math> of the people read both the newspapers, then a possible value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi></math> can be:
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
nA=63

nB=76

nA∩B=x

Let n∪=100

nA∪B=nA+nB−nA∩B≤100

⇒63+76−x≤100

⇒x≥39

But nA∩B≤nA

questions.q: For <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>α</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>N</mi></math>, consider a relation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>R</mi></math> on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>N</mi></math> given by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo></math>{<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfenced><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>:</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>α</mi><mi>y</mi></math> is a multiple of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>7</mn></math>}. The relation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>R</mi></math> is an equivalence relation if and only if
options: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>4</mn></math>is the remainder when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>α</mi></math> is divided by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>10</mn></math>

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>4</mn></math> is the remainder when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>α</mi></math> is divided by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>7</mn></math>
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given, a relation R on N given by R={x,y:3x+αy is a multiple of 7},

Now for R to be reflexive ⇒xRx

⇒3x+αx=7x

⇒3+αx=7K

⇒3+α=7λ

⇒α=7λ-3=7 N+4, where K,λ,N∈I

So, when α divided by 7, remainder is 4.

Now R to be symmetric xRy⇒yRx

3x+αy=7N1,3y+αx=7N2

⇒3+αx+y=7N1+N2=7N3

Which holds when 3+α is multiple of 7

So, α=7N+4 (as did earlier)

Now, for R to be transitive

xRy & yRz⇒xRz.

⇒3x+αy=7N1 ....1 

⇒3y+αz=7N2 ......2

And 3x+αz=7N3 .....3

Now subtracting equation 3-2 we get, 

3x+7N2-3y=7N3

Now putting the value of 3x from equation 1 we get, 7N1-αy+7N2-3y=7N3

⇒7N1+N2-3+αy=7N3

⇒3+αy=7N

Which is true again when 3+α divisible by 7, i.e. when α divided by 7, remainder is 4 .

questions.solution:

a,b=c,d⇒ad=bc

4,3=c,d ⇒ 4d=3c

⇒43=cd

cd=43 & c,d∈2,3,……,30

c, d =4,3,8,6,12,9,16,12,20,15,24,18,28,21

No. of ordered pair =7

questions.q: An organization awarded <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>48</mn></math> medals in event <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mmultiscripts><mi>A</mi><none/><mo>'</mo><mprescripts/><none/><mo>'</mo></mmultiscripts></math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>25</mn></math> in event <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mmultiscripts><mi>B</mi><none/><mo>'</mo><mprescripts/><none/><mo>'</mo></mmultiscripts></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>18</mn></math> in event <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mmultiscripts><mi>C</mi><none/><mo>'</mo><mprescripts/><none/><mo>'</mo></mmultiscripts></math>. If these medals went to total <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>60</mn></math> men and only five men got medals in all the three events, then, how many received medals in exactly two of three events?
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let A, B and C denote the set of men who received medals in even A, event B and event C respectively.

Then, nA=48, nB=25, nC=18 , nA∪B∪C=60 and nA∩B∩C=5,

Now we know that, nA∪B∪C=nA+nB+nC-nA∩B-nA∩C-nB∩C+nA∩B∩C

⇒60=48+25+18-n(A∩B)-n(A∩C)-n(B∩C)+5

⇒n(A∩B)+n(A∩C)+n(A∩C)=48+25+18+5-60=36

Therefore, the number of people who received medals in exactly two of the three sports will be 36-3A∩B∩C=36-15=21.

questions.q:
Let R1 and R2 be two relations defined as follows :

R1=a, b∈R2:a2+b2∈Q and R2=a, b∈R2:a2+b2∉Q, where Q is the set of all rational numbers, then
options: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> is transitive but <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> is not transitive.
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
For R1 let a=1+2, b=1-2, c=814

aR1b⇒a2+b2=1+22+1-22=6∈Q

bR1c⇒b2+c2=1-22+8142=3∈Q

aR1c⇒a2+c2=1+22+8142=3+42∉Q

∴R1 is not transitive.

For R2 let a=1+2, b=2, c=1-2

aR2b⇒a2+b2=1+22+22=5+22∉Q

bR2c⇒b2+c2=22+1-22=5-22∉Q

aR2c⇒a2+c2=1+22+1-22=6∈Q

∴R2 is not transitive.

questions.q: Which of the following is not correct for relation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>R</mi></math> on the set of real numbers?
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:

Then, the number of elements in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>R</mi></math> is
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given b=pq where p & q are prime numbers ≥3 and 1≤pq≤60

If p=3,q=3,5,7,11,13,17,19

And if p=5   q=5,7,11 and so on,

So, b will be 3×3,3×5,3×7,3×11,3×13,3×17,3×19,5×5,5×7,5×11,7×7

i.e. total 11 possibilities

Now a can be 1,2,⋯,60

i.e. total 60 possibilities

Hence, the number of relations =60×11=660

questions.q: Let <math><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi> </mi><mi>B</mi></math> and <math><mi>C</mi><mi> </mi></math> be sets such that <math><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>⊆</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>.</mo></math> Then which of the following statements is not true?
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
For A=C,A-C=ϕ
⇒ϕ⊆B
But A⊈B
Hence, If (A-C)⊆B, then A⊆B is not true
Let x∈ C,  ⇒x∈C∪A∩C∪B
⇒x∈C∪A  and x∈C∪B
⇒(x∈C  or x∈A) and (x∈C or  x∈B)
⇒ x∈C or  x∈A∩B
⇒x∈C or x∈C  as A∪B⊆C
⇒x∈C
⇒C∪A∩C∪B⊆C .... (i)
Now x∈C⇒x∈C∪A and x∈C∪B
⇒x∈(C∪A)∩C∪B
⇒C⊆(C∪A)∩C∪B ..... (ii)
⇒ From (i) and (ii)
C=C∪A∩C∪B
Hence, (C∪A)∩(C∪B)=C is true
Let x∈A  and x∉B
⇒x∈A-B
⇒x∈C  as A-B⊆C
Let x∈A and x∈B
⇒x∈A∩B
⇒x∈C as A∩B⊆C
Hence x∈A ⇒x∈C
⇒A⊆C
Hence, If (A-B)⊆C,  then A⊆C is true
as  C⊇A∩B
⇒B∩C⊇A∩B
as A∩B≠ϕ
⇒B∩C≠ϕ
Hence, B∩C≠ϕ is true

Alternate solution

ϕ≠A∩B⊆C

B=3,4,5

C∪A∩C∪B=1,2,3,4,5,6=C

Option (c) A−B=1,2,3⊆CA⊆C True

Option (d) A−C=ϕ⊆B  A⊆C Not correct

∴ Option (d) is correct

questions.q: Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>…</mo><mo>…</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>18</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mn>77</mn></mrow></mfenced></math> be a set of integers with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>1</mn><mo><</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo><</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo><</mo><mo>…</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo><</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>18</mn></msub><mo><</mo><mn>77</mn></math>. Let the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>:</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> contain exactly <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>39</mn></math> elements. Then, the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mo>…</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>18</mn></msub></math> is equal to ______.
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
If we write the elements of \(A+A\), we can certainly find 39 distinct elements as \(1+1,1+a_1, 1+a_2, \ldots .1\) \(+a_{18}, 1+77, a_1+77, a_2+77, \ldots \ldots a_{18}+77,77+77\). It means all other sums are already present in these 39 values, which is only possible in case when all numbers are in A.P.
Let the common difference be ' \(d\) '.
\(77=1+19 d \Rightarrow d=4\)
So, \(\sum_{i=1}^{18} a_1=\frac{18}{2}\left[2 a_1+17 d\right]=9[10+68]=702\)

questions.q: Set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>A</mi></math> has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>m</mi></math>elements and set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>B</mi></math> has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>n</mi></math>elements. If the total number of subsets of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>A</mi></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>112</mn></math> more than the total number of subsets of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>B</mi></math>, then the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>m</mi><mo>·</mo><mi>n</mi></math> is___.
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
2m=2n+112
⇒2m-2n=112
⇒2n·2m-n-1=24·23-1
⇒n=4, m=7

questions.q: Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced close="}" open="{"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfenced></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced close="}" open="{"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfenced></math> be a relation on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>A</mi></math>. Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>S</mi></math> be the equivalence relation on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>A</mi></math> such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>R</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mi>S</mi></math> and the number of elements in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>S</mi></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>n</mi></math>. Then, the minimum value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>n</mi></math> is _______
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

A=1, 2, 3, 4 and R=(1, 2), (2, 3), (1, 4) be a relation on A.

Now, given S be the equivalence relation on A and R⊂S

So, for S to be equivalence it should be Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive on given relation,

Now, for reflexive Relation we need, 1,1, 2,2, 3,3, 4,4→4 elements,

For Symmetric relation we need, 2,1, 3,2, 4,1→3 elements,

And for Transitive relation we need, 1,3, 3,1, 3,4, 4,2, 2,4, 4,3→6 elements

So, minimum 13 elements should be added in R

Hence , nS=16 elements.

questions.q: Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced close="}" open="{"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfenced></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>R</mi></math> be a relation on the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>A</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>A</mi></math> defined by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced close="}" open="{"><mrow><mfenced><mrow><mfenced><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mfenced><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mo>:</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfenced></math>. Then the number of elements in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>R</mi></math> is _________.
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

Set A=1,2,3,4

And relation on A×A as 2a+3b=4c+5d

Now, Maximum value of 2a+3b=20 at 4, 4

And Minimum value of 4c+5d=9 at 1, 1

So, 4c+5d can be equal to 9, 13, 14, 17, 18, 19

Now 2a+3b can be 9 if a, b=3, 1⇒c, d=1, 1

Similarly, 2a+3b can be 13, if a, b=2, 3⇒c, d=2, 1

And 2a+3b can be 14, if a, b=4, 2  or 1, 4

⇒c, d=1, 2

Similarly, 2a+3b can be 17, if a, b=4, 3⇒ c, d=3, 1

And 2a+3b can be 18 if a, b=3, 4⇒

c, d=2, 2

Hence, there are total 6 elements which satisfy the given relation.

questions.q: The number of relations on the set $\mathrm{A}=\{1,2,3\}$ containing at most 6 elements including $(1,2)$, which are reflexive and transitive but not symmetric, is ________
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& A=\{1,2,3\} \\ & (1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,2) \in R
\end{aligned}$
Remaining elements are
$(2,1),(2,3),(1,3),(3,1),(3,2)$
(1) If relation contains exactly 4 elements = 1 way
(2) if relation contains exactly 5 elements
It can be $(1,3),(3,2) \Rightarrow 2$ ways
(3) If relation contain exactly 6 elements
It can be $((2,3),(1,3)),((1,3),(3,2)),((3,1),(3,2))$
$\Rightarrow 3$ ways.
Total $=6$ ways
